blocks.text: This topic sits at the boundary between cleaning and modeling. Standardization is not fixing an error in the data, it is putting already clean numeric features onto a common scale so downstream algorithms behave correctly. The deeper scaling technique comparisons live in the Machine Learning Fundamentals course's dedicated Feature Scaling module, this topic focuses on standardization itself, the most common technique to know at the data cleaning stage.

Many algorithms, K nearest neighbors, K means clustering, and gradient descent based models like linear regression, logistic regression, and neural networks, are sensitive to the SCALE of input features. A feature measured in thousands, like income, will dominate distance calculations or gradient updates over a feature measured in single digits, like number of children, even if the smaller scale feature is equally or more important.
Standardization transforms a feature so it has a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1, using the formula z equals x minus the mean, all divided by the standard deviation.

items: mean: the average of the whole column.
standard deviation: a measure of how spread out the values are.

blocks.text: Column values: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. Mean is 30. Standard deviation is approximately 14.14.
The resulting z score column genuinely has mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

code.content:
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

scaler = StandardScaler()
scaler.fit(train_df[['col']])                  # learn mean and std from TRAINING data only
train_df['col_z'] = scaler.transform(train_df[['col']])
test_df['col_z'] = scaler.transform(test_df[['col']])   # apply the SAME learned parameters

blocks.text: StandardScaler stores the mean and standard deviation it learned from the training data, so the exact same transformation can correctly be applied later to new, unseen data, like a validation or test set. Manual pandas computation does not do this automatically, this fit then transform pattern is important to understand even at an introductory level.
5. The Critical Rule: Fit Only on Training Data

blocks.title: A subtle form of data leakage
blocks.content: Fitting the scaler on the full dataset, including test data, lets information from the test set leak into the mean and standard deviation used to scale the training data. This makes a model look better during evaluation than it will actually perform on genuinely new data.

blocks.text: Distance based and gradient based algorithms need standardization. Tree based models, like decision trees and random forests, do NOT need it, since a tree split does not care about the absolute scale of a feature, only its relative ordering. Worth knowing this distinction to avoid unnecessary work.

items: Fitting the scaler on the combined train and test data instead of training data alone.
Forgetting to apply the SAME fitted scaler to new data at prediction time, fitting a new scaler on that new data would use a different mean and standard deviation and produce inconsistent results.
Fit the scaler only on training data.
Apply the same fitted scaler to validation and test data, never refit.
Skip standardization for tree based models, it is unnecessary work.
Remember z score standardization centers at 0 with unit variance, it does not bound values to a fixed range like 0 to 1.
